0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

The psalmist of this psalm belonged to a clan of the tribe of Levi whose members led the Israelites in worship and composed many worship songs. The superscription to this psalm describes them as if they were actual **sons** or first-generation descendants of **Korah**, who was a great-grandson of Levi. They were instead later descendants of Korah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [of the descendants of Korah] or [of the Korahites]

1.q: כְּ⁠אַיָּ֗ל תַּעֲרֹ֥ג עַל־אֲפִֽיקֵי־מָ֑יִם כֵּ֤ן נַפְשִׁ֨⁠י תַעֲרֹ֖ג אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ אֱלֹהִֽים
1.note: The psalmist is using one part of himself, his **soul** or inner being, to mean all of him in the act of desiring God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [As a deer pants for streams of water, so in my inner being I pant for you, God]

1.q: כְּ⁠אַיָּ֗ל תַּעֲרֹ֥ג עַל־אֲפִֽיקֵי־מָ֑יִם כֵּ֤ן נַפְשִׁ֨⁠י תַעֲרֹ֖ג אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ אֱלֹהִֽים
1.note: The point of this comparison is that just as a **deer**, when it is very thirsty in a dry place, **pants** desperately for water, so the psalmist desperately desires God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [As a deer pants desperately for streams of water, so in my inner being I pant desperately for you, God]

1.q: כְּ⁠אַיָּ֗ל תַּעֲרֹ֥ג עַל־אֲפִֽיקֵי־מָ֑יִם כֵּ֤ן נַפְשִׁ֨⁠י תַעֲרֹ֖ג אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ אֱלֹהִֽים
1.note: The psalmist is speaking as if his soul were actually panting or taking short, quick breaths. He means that in his inner being, he is desperately feeling and expressing a desire for God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [As a deer pants desperately for streams of water, so in my inner being I desperately desire you, God]

2.note: See how you translated the expression “my soul” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [In my inner being, I thirst for God]

The psalmist is speaking as if he felt physical thirst for God. He is using this image to depict his great desire for God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In my inner being, I feel a great desire for God]

The psalmist is using the question form to express a strong desire. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I want very much to come and appear to the face of God!]
Here, **face** represents “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of God]

As 42:4 and 43:4 suggest, the psalmist is speaking of coming into the presence of God to mean coming into God’s temple. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in God’s temple again]

3.note: The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to represent food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My weeping is my food]

The psalmist is speaking as if he were actually eating his **weeping**. He means that he has been weeping so much that he has been unable to eat. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Instead of eating, I have been weeping]

The psalmist is using the two main components of time, **day** and **night**, to mean all of time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the time]

The psalmist does not indicate specifically who has been **saying** what he quotes. To make clear that someone else, not the psalmist, has been saying this, the ULT supplies the indefinite pronoun **their**. It may be natural in your language to do something similar. You could also use a general expression. Alternate translation: [as they say to me] or [as people say to me]

The psalmist is saying **all the day** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [constantly]

The psalmist’s enemies are using the question form to mock him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Your God certainly does not appear to be helping you!]

4.note: The psalmist is using a verbal form that expresses a resolution. In your translation, use an appropriate verbal form to indicate this. Alternate translation: [I will remember these, and I will pour out my soul within me]

The phrases **Let me remember these** and **let me pour out my soul within me** together express a single idea. The second phrase describes the circumstances under which the psalmist is encouraging himself to do what the first phrase describes. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [Let me remember these as I pour out my soul within me] or [I will remember these as I pour out my soul within me]

The psalmist is using the demonstrative adjective **these** as a noun to mean things of a certain kind, the things he describes in the rest of the verse Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the following things]

The psalmist is speaking as if his **soul** were actually a liquid that he could **pour out**. He is encouraging himself to give full expression, in his own private reflections (**within me**), to what he is feeling deeply in his inner being. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and let me fully express to myself what I am feeling deep inside] or [as I fully express to myself what I am feeling deep inside]

4.q: בַּ⁠סָּךְ֮ אֶדַּדֵּ֗⁠ם עַד־בֵּ֥ית אֱלֹ֫הִ֥ים בְּ⁠קוֹל־רִנָּ֥ה וְ⁠תוֹדָ֗ה הָמ֥וֹן חוֹגֵֽג
4.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put together the information that this **crowd** was **a multitude celebrating a festival**. Alternate translation: [with the crowd, a multitude celebrating a festival. I led them in procession to the house of God with a voice of rejoicing and praise]
See how you translated the term “house” in 5:7. Alternate translation: [the temple of God]

The psalmist is using the **voice** that each person in the **crowd** used for shouting to represent the shouts of the crowd. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with shouts of rejoicing and praise]

5.note: At the end of 42:5 and the beginning of 42:5, the ULT translates the traditional written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. It is different from the other two occurrences of the refrain of this psalm in 42:11 and 43:5. It appears that a verse division has been placed in the middle of a word, so that the prefix that means “and” in those two verses has become a suffix that means “his” in this verse. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. Alternate translation: [the salvation of my face and my God]

The psalmist is speaking as if his **soul** had actually **bowed** itself **down** and as if it were actually **clamoring** or making noises **within** him that indicated how upset it was. He is describing his own inner feelings of despondency and agitation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why do I feel so despondent and agitated inside]

The psalmist is using the question form to give himself a mild rebuke and to encourage himself to consider his situation from a different perspective and so come to feel differently about it. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I do not have to feel so despondent and agitated inside!]

The word that the ULT translates as **Wait** can mean simply not to do something until a certain time has passed or a certain other event has occurred. However, in many biblical contexts, it means to expect that God will do something to change an unfavorable situation that a person cannot change or that a person therefore should not try to change himself, and that is the meaning here. You may be able to use a different term to express this meaning in your language. Alternate translation: [Hope in God] or [I can hope in God]

Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [after all,]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation, following the alternative reading of the ancient Greek translation: [the one who saves my face] or [the savior of my face]

The psalmist is using one part of himself, his **face**, to mean all of him in the act of receiving God’s salvation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation, following the alternative reading of the ancient Greek translation: [the one who saves me] or [my savior]

6.note: See the explanation in a note to the previous verse of how this expression was likely put at the start of this verse when a verse division was mistakenly placed in the middle of a word. You may wish to put this expression at the end of the previous verse, as many versions do, so that the refrain of this psalm will be the same in all three of its occurrences.
See how you translated the similar expression in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [I do feel despondent]

The psalmist may be using the plural term **Hermons** because: (1) Mount Hermon has three distinct peaks. Alternate translation: [and Mount Hermon] or (2) he is referring to the range of mountains that includes Mount Hermon. Alternate translation: [and the Hermon mountain range]

**Mount Mizar** seems to have been the psalmist’s specific location within the general area he describes in the earlier part of this verse. It is not known to what mountain he was referring, so it is not possible to associate it with a mountain that is known by another name today. We therefore recommend that you use the name Mount Mizar in your translation.

7.note: The psalmist is speaking as if the **sound** of the **waterfalls** he hears in the nearby forming Jordan River were actually one **Deep** (one large mass of water) **calling** to another such **deep**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. You could also express this image as a comparison, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [The powerful streams in the river make loud, echoing sounds as they flow over rock ledges as waterfalls]

The terms **breakers** and **waves** mean similar things. The term **waves** describes swellings of water that move across the surface of the ocean, and the term **breakers** describes those swellings as they crash onto the shore. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [As your waves break on the shore, the surf pounds me]

The psalmist is speaking as if he were actually in an ocean or on its shore and strong **waves** and **breakers** were crashing over him, tossing him about. He is representing how overwhelmed he feels. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. You could also express this image as a comparison, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [I am feeling overwhelmed by what you have allowed to happen]

8.q: יוֹמָ֤ם ׀ יְצַוֶּ֬ה יְהוָ֨ה ׀ חַסְדּ֗⁠וֹ וּ֭⁠בַ⁠לַּיְלָה שיר⁠ה עִמִּ֑⁠י
8.note: As in verse 3, the psalmist is using the two main components of time, **day** and **night**, to mean all of time. See how you translated the expression “day and night” in verse 3. It would be appropriate to use similar language here, since the psalmist’s recognition of Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness and his celebration of it in worship are his intentional responses to the sorrow he described earlier. Alternate translation: [Yahweh commands his covenant faithfulness all the time, and his song is with me all the time]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh acts toward me in a way that is faithful to his covenant]

Since the psalmist is referring to a continual activity, he is likely not referring to one specific **song** that expresses one specific **prayer**. He probably means all of the songs that Yahweh enables him to compose in order to sing prayers to him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [his songs are with me, prayers]

The psalmist is speaking of this **song** as if it were a living thing that could be **with** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he enables me to compose songs, prayers]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to indicate that it is **God** who has given him **life** and who preserves his life. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who has given me life] or [the God who preserves my life]

9.note: As in 42:4, the psalmist is using a verbal form that expresses a resolution. See how you translated the similar form there. Alternate translation: [I will say]
See how you translated the term “rock” in 18:2. Alternate translation: [who keeps me safe]

9.q: לָ⁠מָ֪ה שְׁכַ֫חְתָּ֥⁠נִי לָֽ⁠מָּה־קֹדֵ֥ר אֵלֵ֗ךְ בְּ⁠לַ֣חַץ אוֹיֵֽב
9.note: The psalmist is using the question form to express his feelings to God honestly and urgently. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [You appear to have forgotten me! I should not have to walk about mourning because of the oppression of the enemy!]

As in 15:2 and many other places in the Psalms, the psalmist may be using the term **walk** to mean “live.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why do I go through life] or [I should not have to go through life]

As the next verse makes clear, the psalmist is not referring to a specific **enemy**. He means all of the enemies who are oppressing him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [because of the oppression of my enemies]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **oppression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because of the enemies who are oppressing me]

10.note: The psalmist is speaking as if his afflicters were actually **crushing** his **bones**, that is, so badly mistreating him physically that his bones were bruised or broken. He is using this image to represent the deeply painful effect of their **reproach**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In a way that penetrates very painfully into my inner being]

For poetic effect, the psalmist is using again the same phrases that he used in 42:3. We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them there. Alternate translation: [as they say to me constantly, “Your God certainly does not appear to be helping you!”]

11.q: מַה־תִּשְׁתּ֬וֹחֲחִ֨י ׀ נַפְשִׁ⁠י֮ וּֽ⁠מַה־תֶּהֱמִ֪י עָ֫לָ֥⁠י הוֹחִ֣ילִי לֵֽ֭⁠אלֹהִים כִּי־ע֣וֹד אוֹדֶ֑⁠נּוּ יְשׁוּעֹ֥ת פָּ֝נַ֗⁠י וֵֽ⁠אלֹהָֽ⁠י
11.note: This is the second occurrence of the refrain in this psalm. We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them in the first occurrence of this refrain in 42:5. Alternate translation: [I do not have to feel so despondent and agitated inside! I can hope in God. After all, I will again praise him, the one who saves me and who is my God]
